body_en:
## The Niners' 2026 draft class

### Controversial, but with a plan?

The 49ers' complete draft class, with RAS scores, Dane Brugler's evaluations from The Beast and what it all means for the future. You can find our podcast episode about the prospects [here](https://theninerempiregermany.de/ep-373-thank-you-pittsburgh/) (in German).

Back to the draft class: no first-round pick, but a clear statement instead: athleticism first. The 49ers went into draft night with pick 27, traded down twice, first with the Dolphins (#30 + #90), then with the Jets (#33 + #179), and thereby secured three extra picks for day 2 and day 3. The result: a class full of raw, physically impressive players with an average RAS of 9.04. That's no coincidence; that's philosophy.

### What is RAS?

The Relative Athletic Score normalizes all combine measurements (height, weight, speed, explosiveness, agility, strength) on a scale from 0 to 10 and compares each player historically with every athlete ever measured at his position.

### Where does the other information come from?

Dane Brugler's annual draft guide "The Beast" is considered the most accurate publicly available evaluation guide.

## The draft class in detail

### Round 2, pick 33: De'Zhaun Stribling, wide receiver, Ole Miss (RAS 9.57)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| The Beast overall / position | #67 / WR11 |
| 40-yard dash | 4.36 s |
| Height / weight | 6'2" / 207 lbs |
| Career catches / yards / TDs | 216 / 2,964 / 23 |
| Drop rate 2025 | 1.9% |
| Playoff yards per game 2025 | 92.7 avg. |

For some, this pick was a reach: WR11 at pick 33 sounds like an early selection. But anyone who looks at the numbers and the scouting profile understands the logic right away. Stribling's path alone is worth a story: he grew up in Hawaii and played his college career at three different programs (Washington State, Oklahoma State, Ole Miss). In 2025 he led Ole Miss into the College Football Playoff and dominated there with an **average of 92.7 receiving yards** per game.

In 56 college games over five years: 2,964 yards, 23 touchdowns, a 4.36 40 time. And a drop rate of just 1.9 percent in the 2025 season: the man simply doesn't drop the ball. Before the draft, he also received the 49ers' internal **Gold Helmet designation**, awarded for work ethic, character and football IQ to only 16 of all the candidates evaluated. Rare, and a clear indication of why Lynch and Shanahan didn't want to wait for a later pick.

In context, his role is clear: with the trade of Deebo Samuel and, at the latest, the departure of Jauan Jennings, the 49ers lost their physical, versatile receiver. Analysts see Stribling as a natural successor, a "supercharged Jauan Jennings" who combines a vertical threat with a run-blocking-first mindset.

**Dane Brugler, The Beast 2026:** Stribling does the dirty work in run blocking without complaint, a non-negotiable criterion for receivers in Shanahan's wide zone system. Competitive toughness, pro-ready mindset. Projected as a reliable WR2/WR3 with upside for more.

His route tree still has gaps: hitches and go routes made up 57% of his routes, and that has to broaden. But with a RAS of 9.57 and the right coaching staff in Santa Clara, there is enough upside to develop him into a real starting receiver in the long run.

Finally, to what the media consider the most important question: was Stribling a reach, and how big a one?

Pick 33 for a player ranked #67 looks like a clear reach at first, especially since other, much higher-ranked players were still available. However, on The Athletic Football Show's live podcast right after the pick, Dane Brugler was not surprised. After talking with team officials, he had assumed that Stribling would be selected at some point in the second round. Experts such as Nate Tice, Matt Harmon, Lance Zierlein and Albert Breer also confirmed the impression that Stribling was a late riser in the draft process and that several teams rated him much higher than the so-called draft consensus.

Beyond that, it can be assumed that John Lynch and Kyle Shanahan know their colleagues well, especially those they worked with for a long time (Adam Peters, Matt Ryan, the LaFleur brothers, McVay, etc.), and can therefore judge well how high other teams were on Stribling. Based on the information after the draft, it can be assumed that he would no longer have been available at pick #58.

### Round 3, pick 70: Romello Height, edge rusher, Texas Tech (RAS 8.84)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| The Beast overall / position | #80 / EDGE (R3 grade) |
| 40-yard dash | 4.64 s |
| Height / weight | 6'3" / 239 lbs |
| Pressures 2025 | 62 · FBS #7 · Big 12 #2 |
| Vertical jump | 39" |

The 49ers recorded the fewest sacks in the league in the 2025 season. Height is the direct answer. After six college seasons at four programs (Auburn, USC, Georgia Tech, Texas Tech), he finally fully arrived in Lubbock: **10 sacks and 11.5 TFL** in 2025 alone, plus 62 pressures, seventh in all of FBS and second in the Big 12. Together with David Bailey, the second overall pick of the draft, he formed one of the most dangerous pass-rush duos in college football.

What makes him so valuable: he doesn't need mass to be effective. First-step explosion, sudden hands and a spin move that should still give offensive linemen nightmares in his second year. His 39-inch vertical jump confirms the athletic foundation.

**Dane Brugler, The Beast 2026:** Height is a highly specialized sub-down designated pass rusher with elite explosiveness and quick hands, a perfect complement to Nick Bosa. Height himself: "My first step is my most important weapon."

The catch: at 239 pounds, he is occasionally overpowered in head-to-head run defense. He is not yet a full-time, three-down defensive end. But as a situational pass rusher next to Nick Bosa, on passing downs, as part of a rotation with Mykel Williams and Osa Odighizuwa? Analysts are already dreaming of this third-down package. **A real weapon.**

### Round 3, pick 90: Kaelon Black, running back, Indiana (RAS 9.14)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| The Beast overall / position | #214 / RB10 |
| 40-yard dash | 4.45 s |
| Height / weight | 5'9" / 211 lbs |
| Yards after contact per attempt | 3.47 |
| Rushing yards 2025 | 1,000+ |
| Receptions 2025 | 4 |

Frankly: a Beast ranking of 214 at pick 90 is a discrepancy that jumps out. Brugler had graded Black for rounds 5 to 6. Still, this selection has an internal logic, and its name is Christian McCaffrey. Black and Roman Hemby were **the only FBS duo** in which both running backs cracked the 1,000-yard mark in 2025, as part of Indiana's run to the national title.

What sets him apart: he runs physically far above his weight class. **3.47 yards after contact per attempt** means power running, low pad level, natural balance. The man produces more than the play design gives him. At James Madison, where he started together with coach Cignetti, he made the **Paul Hornung Award honor roll** for a strong sophomore season and showed back then that he can also function as a pass catcher: in 2023 alone he caught 27 passes for 254 yards and 4 touchdowns.

At Indiana, he then disappeared from the passing game, not because he lacked the ability, but because the scheme simply didn't call for it. Four catches in 2025 sounds like a red flag, but Black himself explains it soberly: "It kind of got schemed out. We had some great receivers at IU, and the ball was going to them. But it's not like we running backs couldn't do it, we always stayed ready."

**Dane Brugler, The Beast 2026:** Black runs with light feet and consistently gets more out of a play than the design allows. The missing passing-game output at Indiana was a scheme issue, not a talent issue; his past at JMU tells a different story.

### Round 4, pick 107: Gracen Halton, defensive tackle, Oklahoma (RAS 8.45)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| 10-yard split | 1.70 s |
| 40-yard dash | 4.82 s |
| Vertical jump | 36.5" |
| Height / weight | 6'2" / 293 lbs |

The 49ers' sack problem isn't only being addressed from the outside: Halton is the solution up the middle. The key number: **a 10-yard split of 1.70 seconds at almost 300 pounds.** That is the basic requirement for an interior pass rusher who puts offensive linemen under pressure in the first fractions of a second, before the quarterback has finished his drop. Halton's strength lies in his explosiveness, not in sheer mass. A really solid find in round 4 with a RAS of 8.45.

**Dane Brugler, The Beast 2026:** Dane Brugler describes Gracen Halton as a highly efficient rotational player with a "win early and clean up late" style, who above all impresses with his outstanding quickness off the snap. Because of his compact frame and below-average arm length, however, he lacks stability against double teams, which is why in the NFL he is valuable primarily in a part-time role as a penetrating 3-technique tackle. His NFL comparison is none other than Osa Odighizuwa.

Halton is a special pick for us, and of course for David, since he got to announce him on stage.

### Round 4, pick 127: Carver Willis, offensive guard, Washington (RAS 7.93)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| The Beast position | OG20 |
| 40-yard dash | 5.11 s |
| Bench press | 23 reps |
| Broad jump | 9'0" · 108 inches |
| Height / weight | 6'5" / 303 lbs |

Willis is the classic late bloomer of this draft class. Hardly a topic at Kansas State, he transferred to the Washington Huskies and played a super-senior season that forced NFL scouts to take notice. He is strong on the move: he reliably reaches linebackers at the second level and has the strength to roll them out of the way.

**Dane Brugler, The Beast 2026:** Willis shines on the move, exactly what zone blocking systems like the 49ers' demand. As a guard, he still needs to improve his pad-level discipline and reaction speed in tight spaces.

In the short term, Willis is slated as a depth piece and rotational guard. In the long run, though, he could become more relevant: Jake Brendel's contract expires after this season, and Willis brings the athleticism and interior versatility to also be an option at center in the medium term. Not a firm plan, but an interesting thought behind this pick.

### Round 4, pick 139: Ephesians Prysock, cornerback, Washington (RAS 9.74)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| The Beast position | CB18 |
| 40-yard dash | 4.45 s |
| Arm length | 33+ inches |
| Height / weight | 6'3" / 196 lbs |
| Completion rate allowed 2025 | 40.7% |
| Coverage snaps 2025 | 447 |

If there is one player in this draft who will really make 49ers fans sit up in two to three years, it's Ephesians Prysock. The name is unforgettable, and so is the profile. **6'3", more than 33-inch arms, a 4.45 40 time.** For a cornerback, those are measurables that are rare even at an All-Pro level. Prysock first played at Arizona, then transferred to Washington and in 2025 added a spot on the Big Ten All-Academic team to his football honors (honorable mention All-Big Ten).

In 447 coverage snaps in 2025, he allowed a completion rate of only **40.7%**. Opponents preferred to throw elsewhere. And unlike many physical corners, according to PFF he can perform in both man and zone coverage; his 73.2 PFF coverage grade in zone in 2025 is a strong signal.

**Dane Brugler, The Beast 2026:** Prysock is a physical diamond in the rough who can carry receivers vertically and, thanks to his 33+ inch arms, close passing windows even when he is half a step behind the receiver. Areas to work on: too much hand-fighting, and he still lacks trust in his technique.

Getting this athlete in round 4? **That's the potential steal of this draft.**

### Round 5, pick 154: Jaden Dugger, linebacker, Louisiana (RAS 9.60)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| The Beast position | LB · 7th round / priority FA |
| RAS rank among LBs | #139 of 3,460 (since 1987) |
| 40-yard dash | 4.60 s |
| Arm length / wingspan | 35 inches · 7-foot wingspan |
| Height / weight | 6'4" / 242 lbs |
| Tackles / TFL / sacks 2025 | 125 / 13 / 4 |

Dugger is perhaps the craziest story of this entire draft. He started as a **zero-star recruit at Georgetown** (FCS!), moved to Louisiana at the FBS level, first played as a hybrid safety/edge and moved fully inside in 2025. The result: 125 tackles, 13 TFL, 4 sacks, and a missed tackle rate of just 11.6% over his entire career.

**Dane Brugler, The Beast 2026:** "Go-go-gadget arm length": 35 inches for a linebacker is simply extraordinary. An athletic outlier who makes plays through pure reaction and reach. Once he is kept clean of blockers, he practically explodes through his hips when tackling.

With a RAS of 9.60 (rank 139 of 3,460 linebackers tested since 1987), he is an absolute athletic outlier. The linebacker profile is still relatively fresh: instincts, scheme IQ and communication in the huddle need time. But as a day-1 special teams player and long-term development project: **a real fifth-round find.**

### Round 5, pick 179: Enrique Cruz Jr., offensive tackle, Kansas (RAS 9.99)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| The Beast overall / position | #234 / OT |
| 40-yard dash | 4.94 s |
| Broad jump | 9'0" · 108 inches |
| Height / weight | 6'6" / 313 lbs |

A RAS of **9.99 out of 10.00**: almost perfect on paper. 6'6", 313 pounds, a 9-foot broad jump and a 4.94 40 time for an offensive tackle of this size. No player in his position group comes anywhere close to this combination of frame and athleticism.

**Dane Brugler, The Beast 2026:** Before the 2025 season, Cruz was barely on most teams' radar ("barely graded") and forced the scouts' attention with consistently solid performances. Vice-grip hands, but his timing and hand technique still need work.

In round 5, you gladly take this athletic promise. As a practice squad project that can mature in peace and secure depth at tackle in the long run.

## Undrafted free agents (UDFAs)

An NFL front office's work doesn't end with the last draft pick. The 49ers were extremely aggressive on the UDFA market, and that shows not only in the number of signings but also in some unusually high guarantees.

| Player | Position, college | RAS | Measurables | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Khalil Dinkins | TE, Penn State | 7.82 | 6'3" · 251 lbs · 4.72 s | Athletic TE with real speed for his size; $275,000 guaranteed |
| James Thompson Jr. | DT, Illinois | 8.94 | 6'5" · 308 lbs · 5.00 s | Massive nose tackle with an exceptional RAS for his size; $280,000 guaranteed |
| Wesley Grimes | WR, NC State | 9.32 | 6'2" · 194 lbs | 77 rec. / 1,121 yds / 9 TDs · Beast WR85 |
| Will Pauling | WR, Notre Dame | 7.05 | 5'10" · 183 lbs · 4.37 s | 1,753 yds / 15 TDs · speed specialist |
| Jalen Stroman | FS, Notre Dame | 4.57 | 6'1" · 203 lbs | 111 tackles at Virginia Tech · pre-injury: day-3 grade |
| Bryson Eason | DT, Tennessee | 6.94 | 6'2" · 323 lbs | Beast DT20 · 6 seasons · 105 tackles / 4.5 sacks |
| Mikail Kamara | EDGE, Indiana | 2.15 | 6'1" · 250 lbs | 127 pressures in 2 seasons · production beats measurables |
| Jack Bouwmeester | P, Texas | – | 6'2" · 193 lbs | 43.5-yard punting average in college |

### Khalil Dinkins and James Thompson Jr.: a statement

$275,000 and $280,000 in guarantees for UDFAs often exceed the guaranteed portion of a seventh-round deal. These amounts aren't random: they reflect high internal grades and show that the front office really wanted these players. Thompson brings a RAS of 8.94 as an almost 310-pound tackle, an exceptional value for his position group. Dinkins' 40 time of 4.72 seconds for a tight end of his size also explains the interest by itself.

### Mikail Kamara: production beats measurables

Kamara is one of the most fascinating scouting puzzles of this class. A RAS of 2.15 says: too small, not explosive enough for an NFL edge. But his tape tells a different story: **127 combined pressures in two seasons** at Indiana. He plays with an extremely high motor, understands how to compensate for his physical limits and has a feel for when to counter instead of pushing straight ahead. Brugler writes: "You feel his impact during games," a rare compliment for a UDFA.

## Conclusion

No pick in round 1, yet one of the 49ers' most athletic draft classes in years. The average RAS of the eight draft picks:

**Average RAS: 9.04**

That is a clear signal. John Lynch and the front office made a conscious decision: in a draft considered rather weak, they preferred raw athletic traits and lots of college experience over young wild cards.

The pattern is unmistakable: Prysock (9.74), Dugger (9.60), Cruz (9.99). Rounds 4 and 5 bring athletes who can keep up with first-round picks on physical parameters. Height and Halton directly address the pass-rush deficit. Stribling finally brings the blocking receiver that Shanahan's scheme demands. On the UDFA market, two players with unusually high guarantees were secured in Dinkins ($275k) and Thompson ($280k).

There is risk. Black was a reach. Dugger and Cruz are real development projects. But this coaching staff in Santa Clara is capable of anything and deserves the benefit of the doubt for now.

This class will have to be judged in three years. The foundations are right, and the plan sounds promising.
